newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania Socialists see win over president's party.
newsitem.headline: Albania Socialists see win over president's party.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party and the opposition Socialists both forecast victory on Sunday in an early general election intended to end months of violence in the Balkan nation.

With partial official results trickling in slowly, the two major parties cited their own data to show they had won large numbers of seats in the 155-seat parliament. But jubilation at Socialist headquarters contrasted with long faces among top Berisha stalwarts, reflecting possible heavy losses.
Albania's Interior Ministry warned people in messages flashed on television screens not to stage street celebrations, particularly in Tirana's central Skanderbeg Square.
Armed police took up positions nearby and armoured vehicles patrolled major streets. But there was only slightly more than the isolated shooting that erupts in Tirana each evening.
Both Berisha and Socialist leader Fatos Nano, who blames the president for months of upheaval in which about 1,500 people have died, pledged to respect whatever outcome voting produced.
The Socialists said they had captured two-thirds of the popular vote and were preparing to form the next government.
"Today there are no losers, only winners," Socialist spokesman Kastriot Islami told reporters. "We will first of all appeal to everyone to put down their weapons."
Islami said the Socialists had won 11 of 15 seats in Tirana and captured more than 85 percent of the vote in some parts of the south, focal point of the revolt against Berisha.
Early returns gave the Socialists an easy victory in two seats in the southern city of Gjirokaster and an unassailable lead in the Adriatic port of Sarande.

The Democrats said they had won 17 seats in seven areas, including the port of Durres and the central city of Lushnje. But a party statement made no mention of results in Tirana, viewed the key to capturing a parliamentary majority.

Isolated incidents across the Balkan state claimed at least one life, an electoral official killed near the southern town of Fier. But Sunday's voting proceeded without the widespread violence which gripped the country for months.

Socialist supporters in Tirana sang and chanted outside party headquarters. In the south, where gangs denouncing Berisha still control most towns, they fired long volleys into the air after official results showed them far in the lead.

Officials said turnout had been a healthy 65 percent an hour before voting ended. Polls closed at 6 p.m., three hours earlier than originally planned, to ensure safety for voters and some 500 international observers ahead of counting.
A 7,000-strong International Protection Force sent to Albania in April helped to guard polling stations and more than 500 international observers spread across the country.

More than 1,000 candidates from 27 parties stood for the 155 parliamentary seats -- 115 to be decided in two-round majority races and the rest by a proportional system. The Democrats held 122 of the 140 seats in the outgoing parliament.
A second round will be held next Sunday between the the two top candidates in districts where no one won 50 percent of the vote in the first round.

Berisha, president since 1992, said after voting in a polling station in a Tirana school that he would abide by the outcome of the vote. "I am definitely going to accept the results. I...will fully recognise the elections," he said.
But he was circumspect about whether he would stay in office if the Socialists scored a big victory. It was too early, he said, to consider "cohabitation" in Albania.
Nano said the election was "of extraordinary importance" seven years after the collapse of one of eastern Europe's most repressive communist regimes.

Catherine Lalumiere, top official for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe overseeing the vote, toured polling stations in Tirana and provincial towns by helicopter and said she was generally pleased with what she saw.
The OSCE has said it is unrealistic for normal Western standards to be attained in Albania's election.
Both main parties complained of irregularities, mostly voters left off lists. There were also incidents of ballot papers or boxes being stolen or tampered with at gunpoint.
The election campaign was conducted under a state of emergency imposed on March 2 to try to quell the unrest. A 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew was lifted just for election day.
